The History

Walter Hines Page -- 1855–1918

He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

In February 1913, Walter Hines Page purchased a thousand-acre farm southwest of Pinehurst -- land his father Frank had logged a generation before. He named it Garran Hill. The name was inlaid in the threshold brick before ground was broken.

Weeks later, President Woodrow Wilson appointed him U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James's. Page left for London. He directed construction from three thousand miles away. His son Ralph supervised on the ground. Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game." -- Walter Hines Page, letter to Ralph

The house was completed in 1916. He served through the whole of the First World War. He came home in December 1918. His son carried him off the train at Aberdeen.

His last recorded words: "Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"

He died ten days later at Currituck Cottage in Pinehurst. A tablet in the vestibule of Westminster Abbey reads: "The friend of Britain in her sorest need."

Garran Hill · 1916

Inlaid before ground was broken.
Still there.

Betty Dumaine -- 1900–1984

She planted the roses.
She raised the peacocks.
She ran charities from this house.

In 1919, at the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Betty Dumaine met Khun Sangwan Chukramol -- a young Thai woman who would become the Princess Mother of Thailand, mother of two kings.

Forty years later, in 1959, Betty purchased the house. She renamed it Hollycrest. She planted magnolias, camellias, dogwoods. She added stables and kennels for horses, hounds, and peacocks. The Thai royal family knew this house. The Thai royal family bestowed upon her the title Thanpuying.

Someone still puts flowers there.

Blue Fox. MY IRISH HUNTER BLUE FOX 1946–1965. Buried at the back of the property. Slate cover. Brass marker.
